_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 169 - John B. Stair, Old Samoa (London 1897): ch. 9 Mythology and Spirit-lore. Topics 1 creation, 2 deity, 7 cosmology. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Tuli Complains and Tangaloa Fishes Up the Land
title.zh: 鷸鳥啼訴：坦加羅亞釣起大地

region.zh: 薩摩亞上空（象徵性定位）

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: Tangaloa of the Skies, principal god and creator, sent his son the plover Tuli down to the ocean's surface; finding no place to rest, Tuli returned to complain, and Tangaloa threw down a stone which became land - or fished one up from the bottom of the sea with his great fish-hook, raising it higher on a second cast when the waves still wetted Tuli's feet. The reclining rock gave place to the spreading, sitting and upright rocks, then earth and grass and conquering convolvulus - whose rottenness bred the two grubs out of which Ngai-tosi and Ngai-va'a-va'ai shaped the first two bodies of mankind, part by part named for Tuli.
summary.zh: 天主坦加羅亞遣其子——鷸鳥圖利——下探海面；無處棲身，鷸鳥啼訴於天，父乃擲下巨石化為陸地——或以神鉤自海底釣起山岩，浪濤仍濕其足，遂二次揚鉤升高陸地。臥岩讓位於蔓延岩、坐岩、立岩；其後泥土、青草、藤蔓相繼而出——腐藤之中化出兩條幼蟲，恩加伊托西與恩加伊瓦瓦艾將其塑為兩具人形，各部皆冠以圖利之名。

sensitivity.note: Samoan creation; fish-hook parallels the Maori Maui and Hawaiian creation.

passages.text: The Samoans had several superior divinities and a host of inferior ones, and they were also accustomed to deify the spirits of deceased chiefs. Of the primitive gods the chief place is assigned to Tangaloa, or, as he is sometimes called, Tangaloa-langi, Tangaloa of the Skies. He was always spoken of as the principal god, the creator of the world and progenitor of the other gods and mankind. In one tradition that gives an account of the formation of the earth mention is made of other divinities or helpers, Tangaloa-tosi, also styled Ngai-tosi (Ngai the marker), and Ngai-va'a-va'ai (Ngai the seer or beholder), also called Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai; these two helpers are introduced as being sent by Tangaloa to complete the formation of the bodies of the first two of mankind, and to impart life to them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The son of Tangaloa was the Tuli, a species of plover. Tuli went down from the heavens to the surface of the ocean, but found no place on which to rest, and returned to complain to his father. On this his father threw down a stone from the heavens, which became land. Another account of the origin of the earth states that, in answer to Tuli's complaint of want of a resting-place, Tangaloa fished up a large stone from the bottom of the sea with a fish-hook; having raised the stone to the surface, he gave it to his son for his dwelling-place. On going thither to take possession of his new home Tuli found that every wave or swell of the ocean partially overflowed it, which compelled him to hop from one part to another of the stone to prevent his feet being wetted by each succeeding wave; annoyed at this, he returned to the skies to complain to his father, who, by a second application of the mighty fish-hook, raised the land to the desired height. This version is also given by the inhabitants of other groups in Polynesia.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: This tradition also gives the history of the worm of the earth. Popo-taoto, the reclining rock, was succeeded by Popo-sosolo, the spreading rock; Papa-sosolo was succeeded by Papa-nofo, the sitting rock; Papa-nofo was succeeded by Papa-tu, the upright rock. The rock was succeeded by the earth or mould, which was then spread over with grass; after this the fue (convolvulus) grew and overcame the grass. Tuli returned to his father, Tangaloa, having obtained his land, but there was no man to reside on it. His father said to him, 'You have got your land. What grows on it?' Tuli answered, 'The fue.' His father told him to go and pull it up, which he did, and on its rotting produced two grubs, which moved a little as Tuli looked upon them; he again returned to the skies to tell his father of their birth. Upon this Tuli was told to return to the earth and take with him Tangaloa-tosi, or Ngai-tosi, the marker, and Tangaloa-va'a-va'ai, the seer, who were told to operate upon the two grubs; on their arrival they began to form them into the shape of men, commencing at the head. When the head was completed Tuli said, 'Let my name be joined with that of the head', a portion of which was then named O le-tuli-ulu; they then proceeded to give sight by forming the eyes, when Tuli made the same request as before, upon which a portion of the eye was called O le-tuli-mata; the different members of the body were successively formed, each having the name of Tuli prefixed to the portion of the body as formed: as the elbow, O le-tuli-lima, and the knee, O le-tuli-vae.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The First Man Dies by the Little Fish Lo

region.zh: 新成之薩摩亞（象徵性定位）

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: The two shaped bodies lived, but were both males. One day, fishing with a net called the faamutu, one of them was injured by a small fish called the lo, which caused his death. Tuli returned to the skies and bewailed the loss of one of the inhabitants of his land; Ngai-tosi was directed by Tangaloa to proceed to the earth and reanimate the dead body, changing the sex of the deceased male to that of a female - and the two became man and wife, the parents of the human race.
summary.zh: 所塑的兩具身體活了，卻皆為男子。一日以『法阿姆圖圖』漁網捕魚，其一被小魚『羅』所傷而死。圖利上天空哀悼其民之喪；坦加羅亞遣恩加伊托西下界復活屍身——並將死者由男易女。二人遂結為夫婦，成為人類之父母。

sensitivity.note: Origin of death and of the human pair in the Stair recension.

passages.text: On the formation of the two bodies being complete they lived, but were both males, and dwelt on the land on which they were formed. One day, whilst fishing with a net called the faamutu, one of them was injured by a small fish called the lo, which caused his death. Upon this Tuli returned to the skies, and bewailed the loss of one of the inhabitants of his land to his father, when Ngai-tosi was directed by Tangaloa to proceed to the earth and reanimate the dead body; previously to which, however, he changed the sex of the deceased male to that of a female. The two then became man and wife, and the parents of the human race.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: In connexion with this history of Tangaloa it may be mentioned that occasional visits are stated to have been made to the abode of the august Tangaloa by parties from the earth, who returned with some useful benefaction from the deity - as, for instance, Losi, who is reputed to have been the benefactor of his countrymen by bringing taro.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

title.en: The Leaping Stone and the Two Roads of the Dead

region.en: Falealupo, west point of Savaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 薩瓦伊島西端法萊阿盧波（象徵性定位）

source.work: John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (London 1897)

summary.en: The disembodied spirit retains the exact resemblance of its former self and immediately begins its solitary journey to the Fafa, westward of Savaii: from Manuka the ghost swims island to island to the west point of Savaii, where at the leaping-stone all spirits leap into the sea. There are two roads - O le Lua-loto-o-Alii, the deep hole of chiefs, to Pulotu the abode of the blest; and O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua, the deep hole of the common people, to Le nu'u-o-nonoa, the land of the bound, another name for the dreadful Sa-le-Fe'e. Natives have assured Stair that spirits passed them on the road and returned no answer.
summary.zh: 亡魂離體，貌如生前，即刻啟程獨行冥府法法——位於薩瓦伊之西：自毛卡出發的魂靈逐島泅渡，至薩瓦伊西端『躍魂之石』縱身入海。冥途有二：『酋長深穴』通往福地普洛圖；『平民深穴』通往『受縛者之鄉』——即可怖的薩勒費埃。斯泰爾親聞土人說：魂靈曾與他們同行於路，呼之而不應。

sensitivity.note: Samoan eschatology; two-roads parallel to Tongan Pulotu/Sa-le-Fe'e.

passages.text: O le Fafa, Sa-le-Fe'e, and Pulotu are places which occupy a prominent position in Samoan mythology, and seem in some manner to be connected the one with the other. O le Fafa (Hades) is alike the entrance to Sa-le-Fe'e, the Samoan Tartarus, or dread place of punishment, and also to Pulotu, the abode of the blest; the one entrance being called O le Lua-loto-o-Alii, or deep hole of chiefs, by which they passed to Pulotu; the other, O le Lua-loto-o-tau-fanua, or deep hole of the common people, by which they passed to Le nu'u-o-nonoa, or the land of the bound, which is simply another term for the much-dreaded Sa-le-Fe'e. The idea of the superiority of the chiefs over the common people was thus perpetuated, none but chiefs or higher ranks gaining entrance to the Samoan Elysium.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The disembodied spirit was supposed to retain the exact resemblance of its former self, and immediately on leaving the body it was believed to commence its solitary journey to the Fafa, which was located to the westward of Savaii, the most westerly of the group, and towards this point disembodied spirits from all the islands bent their way immediately after death. Thus in case of a spirit commencing its journey at Manuka, the most easterly of the group, it journeyed on to the western end of that island from whence it started, where it dived into the sea and swam to the nearest point of Tutuila, where, having journeyed along the shore to the extreme west point of that island, it again plunged into the sea and pursued its solitary way to the next island, and thus onward throughout the entire group until it reached the extreme west point of Savaii, where it finally dived into the ocean and pursued its solitary way to the mysterious Fafa. At the west point of Upolu the land terminates in a narrow rocky point, which is still known as O le fatu-osofia, the leaping-stone, from which all spirits were said to leap into the sea en route to the Fafa. This was a much-dreaded point, where the lonely travellers were said to be certainly met with, and their company was anything but desired. Many times natives have assured me that disembodied spirits have passed them on the road when travelling; when asked how they knew them, they answered, 'Why, we knew them personally, and spoke to them, but received no answer', which was quite sufficient in their estimation to determine the spiritual nature of the parties met, since it is the invariable custom of the Samoans to return an answer when accosted on a journey - to do otherwise being looked upon as an insult.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.

passages.text: The priesthood, Taula-aitu (anchors of the spirits), were divided into four classes: priests of the war-gods, keepers of the war-gods, family priests, and prophets or sorcerers. The Taula-aitu-o-aitu-tau were important personages, being consulted upon all warlike occasions; this class invoked the assistance of various war-gods, but most of all Nafanua, a female deity who was reverenced by the entire population, and who in conjunction with Savea-se'u-leo may be considered the national gods of war. It was one of this class, the representative of Le Tamafainga, that usurped the regal power of the islands and reigned with great tyranny over the whole of Samoa until the year 1829, when he was slain by the people of A'ana - he was worshipped as combining both regal and divine attributes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of John B. Stair, Old Samoa, ch. 9 (1897); not verbatim.
